TITLE: Global Sensitivity Analysis for High-Dimensional Models using Orthogonal Function Expansions
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether using orthogonal function expansions (e.g., polynomial chaos expansions) to approximate the feature-sum function $v(S)$ in the Shapley value calculation can improve the scalability of global sensitivity analysis for high-dimensional models. This can be done using a fixed set of orthogonal functions, where each function $f_i$ is orthogonal to all the others, and approximating $v(S)$ by a linear combination of such functions, i.e., $v(S) \approx \sum_{i=1}^{N} c_i f_i(S)$.
CONTROLS: Regularized least squares regression on $v(S)$ without expansions as a baseline, or even just naively computing Shapley values on the original high-dimensional input.
COST: 75GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approximation approach could either significantly reduce the computational cost of Shapley value computation, particularly when combined with sparse or adaptive sampling strategies (Success), but in some cases may not capture the most salient features of the original function $v(S)$, which could lead to inaccurate Shapley values (Failure).

The goal is to derive a bound on the expected squared error of the KernelSHAP estimate in terms of the number of samples, the dimensionality of the input, and the smoothness of the function $v(S)$.
CONTROLS: Analyze KernelSHAP using a simpler model where $v(S)$ is a smooth function, and run numerical experiments to compare the obtained convergence bound to its performance in practice.
COST: 105GPU-hours

If the convergence analysis fails to produce reasonable bounds, this might be due to the strong smoothness assumptions made (Failure).

TITLE: Forecasting Future Scenes with Causality-Aware Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We adapt causality-aware diffusion models to the task of satellite image time series forecasting, aiming to generate temporally consistent forecasts by conditioning the diffusion process on the historical sequence and the underlying causal narrative of the changes. Specifically, we draw upon the concept of " temporal causal cloning", which enables the model to learn a potentially invertible transformation from the observed scene to its causally sufficient representation, thereby allowing for a more accurate forecasting of future scenes. The causal cloning is achieved by introducing a graph-based temporal causal model that captures the causal relationships between observations over time.
CONTROLS: Current state-of-the-art diffusion-based models for image generation, our previous proposal for investigating multimodal sampling for temporal evolution description, and a baseline of simple temporal interpolation methods and traditional diffusion models without causal awareness. 
COST: 16368.8
PREDICTION: We expect a significant improvement in temporal consistency, with a forecasting accuracy that surpasses existing baselines by at least 30%, and a notable reduction in errors related to unrealistic changes; however, the model may struggle with complex causal relationships, leading to potential underperformance in scenes with multiple interacting variables.

TITLE: Evaluating Temporal Consistency with a Structural Similarity Metric
PROPOSAL: To rigorously evaluate the temporal consistency of forecasts, we propose a novel structural similarity metric that assesses the similarity between the forecasted scene and its expected evolution based on the historical sequence. This metric combines elements of the Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) and the Structural Similarity Index (SSIM), with an additional term that accounts for the temporal coherence between consecutive frames. We then use this metric to evaluate the performance of our causality-aware diffusion model and existing baselines, providing a more comprehensive understanding of their strengths and weaknesses.
CONTROLS: Current state-of-the-art metrics for image quality and temporal coherence, such as PSNR, SSIM, and Mean Squared Error (MSE), as well as the baselines for our previous experiments.
COST: 1214.1
